Enhancing methane production of anaerobic digested sewage
sludge by advanced wet oxidation & steam explosion
pretreatment

a b s t r a c t
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of sewage sludge is associated with lowered carbon conversion
efficiency due to the recalcitrance of microbial cells in the Waste Activated Sludge (WAS)
from the aeration basins with 50 % of the dry weight still being present after AD. The
effect of Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam Explosion (AWOEx) pretreatment on the
methane yield at variable temperatures (165–200 ◦C), residence time (15–45 min) and
oxygen dosage (1%–10% based on VS concentration) was tested in this study. Central
composite design (JMP
® Pro) was used to design 19 runs of AWOEx pretreatment
of dewatered digested sewage sludge (DADSS) at different operating conditions. After
pretreatment the DADSS was fed to 19 bioreactors operated in semi-continues mode at
37 ◦C. The highest average methane yields of 183 mL/g VS and 170 mL/g VS were found
for the bioreactors receiving DADSS pretreated at 165 ◦C with a retention time of 15 min
and 10 % O2 (Condition 1), and, 182.5 ◦C with a retention time of 15 min and 5.5 % O2
(Condition 2). This corresponds to an increase in the methane production of 156.2 % and
140.5 % compared to the methane production from the DADSS without pretreatment.
Plotting the results using the response surface model showed that temperature and
O2 dosage had a significant effect on the methane yield while residence time was of
lower importance. Importantly, thermic treatment without oxygen showed far lower
methane yields of 114.5 mL/gVS and 120.26 mL/gVS, respectively of the two best
conditions described above. Through this two-step AD process, we were able to achieve
a net 94% improved methane yield compared to conventional AD of sewage sludge by
implementing a second AWOEx pretreatment step (followed by secondary AD) with
26.9% decreased organics content, further reducing the cost of the final disposal of the
treated sewage sludge.

1. Introduction
In United States a total of 6.5 million metric tons per year of dewatered sewage sludge (DSS) is produced in the ca.
15,000 wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) (Nguyen et al., 2021; Seiple et al., 2020). The high organic content of DSS

makes this waste a potential resource for production of bioenergy and biofuels (Shi et al., 2021). Approximately 50% of
all WWTP’s in the US corresponding to a total number of 7500 are converting their sewage sludge to biogas (a mixture
of methane (ca. 60%) and CO2 (ca. 40%)) using anaerobic digestion (AD) (Shi et al., 2021). However, the amount of biogas
produced are often too low to warrant the use of this biogas. If more biogas could be produced from the sewage sludge this
could offset a significant amount of the energy used by WWTPs. Besides, biogas can be upgraded to Renewable Natural
Gas (RNG) and used as a transportation fuel or added to the natural gas grid. A major constraint for producing biogas as
an energy source is the fact that only approximately 50% of the organic material in the sewage sludge will be converted
during conventional AD. It has previously been reported that conventional AD of sewage sludge produce a methane yield
in the range of 0.19 to 0.24 Nm3/Kg VSin (Di Capua et al., 2020). The residual organics after AD needs to be concentrated
by separation and disposed either in landfills, on agricultural land and parks or incinerated (Nguyen et al., 2021). All these
management practices have some specific problems for both the environment and the public.
Typically, the composition of concentrated sewage sludge includes TS (12%–40%), VS (75%–85%), protein (18%–40%),
lipids (6%–19%), lignin (23%–29%), and carbohydrates (10%–15%) (Nguyen et al., 2021; Su et al., 2019). One of the major
reasons for the recalcitrance of sewage sludge during AD is the fact that activated sludge (WAS) is mainly composed of
bacterial cell walls as well as recalcitrant polymers such as cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin (Hao et al., 2020; Nguyen
et al., 2021). Previous studies have shown that the digestate produced after AD is still rich in organics, which have not
been converted during the AD process (Li et al., 2017; Nordell et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020). Several thermal pretreatments
technologies have been developed for enhancing AD of dewatered sewage sludge (Cambi THP, Veolia Exelys) (Abu-Orf and
Goss, 2012; Shi et al., 2021). However, none of these techniques has been applied to DADSS as tested in this study. The
conditions used for both these processes are generally less severe (temperatures of max 160 ◦C) and the biogas yields
improvement are generally moderate around 30%–40% (Nguyen et al., 2021; Seiple et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Yan
et al., 2021).
Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam Explosion pretreatment (AWOEx) is a thermochemical process integrating wet
oxidation and steam explosion (Ahring and Munck, 2013; Miklos et al., 2018; Svensson et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2020).
In this process, biomass is exposed to an oxidizing agents such as air, hydrogen peroxide, pure oxygen etc. under high
temperatures (over 140 ◦C) and pressures (over 10 bars) for the duration of 15 to 45 min (Ahring and Munck, 2013;
Biswas et al., 2015, 2020; M’Arimi et al., 2020). AWOEx pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass materials significantly
enhance lignin solubilization. In addition, crystalline cellulose remains in the solid fraction whereas most hemicellulose
components are solubilized during the process (Biswas et al., 2020; Khan and Ahring, 2020). As a result of AWOEx
pretreatment, the surface area of the biomass is greatly increased, which increases the microbial and enzymatic access
to the carbohydrates in the material (Dewil et al., 2017). Besides, acetic acid is produced via de-esterification of the
acetyl groups, which further influences the dissolution of hemicellulose into the aqueous phase (Biswas et al., 2020,
2014). The advantages of AWOEx pretreatment are besides its effectiveness the fact that no chemicals are added needing
recovery along with a low formation of inhibitory by-products. AWOEx pretreatment can be performed at high dry matter
concentrations of up to 45%, which lower the overall cost of the pretreatment (Biswas et al., 2020).
While AWOEx has been extensively tested for different lignocellulosic biomass materials (Biswas et al., 2015, 2014;
Khan and Ahring, 2020; M’Arimi et al., 2020), the use of the technology for improving the carbon conversion efficiency of
sewage sludge into methane has not been studied in any details. In this study, we will use a central composite statistic
method to determine the optimal pretreatment conditions for AWOEx. We will further determine the composition of
dewatered digested sewage sludge (DADSS) out of the initial AD bioreactor and out of the secondary AD to understand
the effect that the AWOEx pretreatment would have on the biodegradation of the different components of digested sewage
sludge.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstock and composition
Dewatered anaerobic digested sewage sludge (DADSS) was obtained from Walla Walla wastewater treatment plant in
Eastern Washington. The DADSS was collected after dewatering in a filter press. It contained a total solids (TS) of 13.6%;
a moisture content (MC) of 86.4%; and a volatile solid (VS) of 10.6%. All samples of DADSS before and after pretreatment
were stored at 4 ◦C before use.
2.2. Design of experiment
The Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam Explosion (AWOEx) pretreatment of DADSS was performed at temperatures
ranging from 165–200 ◦C, oxygen (O2) dosage from 1%–10% of the VS, and a residence time of between 15 and 45 min.
A central composite design based on statistical analytic system (SAS) (Heng et al., 2021) was utilized to find the optimal
pretreatment process using different dosages of oxygen (between 0%–10%) at temperatures ranging from 165 to 200 ◦C
in a pilot pretreatment reactor (Supaporn and Yeom, 2022). From the model, we defined three AWOEx sets at the
temperatures: 165 ◦C, 182.5 ◦C and 200 ◦C with and without oxygen added and with controls without any pretreatment
(Table 1). The results from a series of 19 runs (3 controls and 16 test sets) with different operating conditions was used
to generate the regression report of the factors and results.

2.3. Advanced wet oxidation & steam explosion pretreatment
AWOEx of DADSS was carried out in a 100 L stainless steel pressure tank. In each run 10 kg dewatered DADSS was
feed into the reactor and kept at a mixing speed of 50 rpm. The target temperature was achieved by steam addition into
the pretreatment reactor while the temperature was kept constant using an external oil heater. Oxygen (O2) was purged
into the reactor based on the amount of VS of DADSS while increasing the mixing speed to 85 rpm. Upon completion of
the residence time, the material was flashed out of the tank and into a 250 L flash tank. After cooling, the sample was
collected and stored at 4 ◦C for further analysis and biogas yield determination.
2.4. Anaerobic digestion of pretreated DADSS
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of DADSS were conducted in a series of 1 L bioreactors, operated in semi-continuous mode
with a working volume of 400 mL. The hydraulic retention time (HRT) was kept at 20 days and all bioreactors were feed
every second day at the exact same time with a recording of the biogas produced. Two reactors containing DADSS without
pretreatment was used as controls.
2.5. Composition analysis
The moisture contents (MC), total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), carbohydrates (cellulose and hemicellulose), lignin,
and lipid content of all DADSS samples before and after AWOEx and AD were measured following the National Renewable
Energy Laboratory (NREL) methods as previous described studies (Biswas et al., 2020; Hames et al., 2008; Van Wychen
et al., 2016). Protein contents of all samples before and after AWOEx of DADSS were measured by the Lowry method
(Amin et al., 2021; Judickaite et al., 2021). NREL standard method was used for determining total lignin (acid soluble
and acid insoluble) and total cellulose and hemicellulose (Sluiter et al., 2008). Acid soluble lignin was determined using a
UV spectrophotometer, whereas total carbohydrates (sum of glucose, xylose, and arabinose) were determined after two-
step hydrolysis (Jenway 6405 UV/Visible, NJ, USA) with a wavelength of 320 nm. Monomers were analyzed by using an
UltiMate
® 3000 HPLC system (Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA) with an Aminex
® 87H Column 250 × 4.6 mm (Bio-Rad, Hercules,
CA) and a Shodex RI-101 refractive index detector at 60 ◦C using 4 mmol H2SO4 as an eluent with a flow rate of 0.6 ml/min.
All measurements of lignin and carbohydrates analysis were done in duplicates. The lipid extraction was performed
following chloroform–methanol extraction method proposed by Bligh and Dyer (1959).1 g of dried sludge were mixed
with 20 mL of mixed liquor (chloroform: methanol = 2:1, v/v) and then subjected to 60 ◦C for 4 h. Thereafter, the mixture
was placed in a centrifuge for 15 min at 3000 rpm and the solvent phase was transferred to a glass vial. After evaporating
the solvent at 60 ◦C, the vial was weighed. The difference in weight was the total lipid content.
2.6. Volatile fatty acids analysis
The concentration of volatile fatty acids was determined in the influent and effluent samples for each bioreactor using
high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) as previously described (Khan and Ahring, 2020). 2 mL of each sample
was taken and centrifuged at 10, 000 RPM for 10 min. The supernatant was separated with pipette, diluted 2 times with
4 mM sulfuric acid and the filtered through 0.2 µm. The samples were analyzed by UltiMate
®3000 HPLC system (Dionex,
Sunnyvale, CA) with an Aminex
®87H column 250 × 4.6 mm (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA) and a Shodex RI-101 refractive index
detector.
2.7. Biogas analysis
The composition of methane and carbon dioxide from all bioreactors were determined using an Universal gas analyzer,
UGA series (Stanford Research Systems, Sunnyvale, CA) (Khan and Ahring, 2020).

2.8. Statistical analysis
The design of the experiments and the experimental data were analyzed using the statistical software (SAS) JMP Pro
(version 15.2.0) (Biswas et al., 2020). The response of temperature, residence time, and oxygen dosage on DADSS was
evaluated using the methane yield obtained from the AD reactors operated under different conditions. The analysis was
conducted on a fitted correlation using 2nd degree interaction under response surface macros and standard least-square
personality with an emphasis on effect leverage (Biswas et al., 2015). The effect of pretreatment on the methane yield
was analyzed through one way ANOVA test.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Composition of DADSS
The characteristics of DADSS are shown in Table 1. DADSS contained 86.44% of moisture contents (MS), 13.56% of total
solids (TS), and 10.6% of volatile solids (VS) which is 77.8% of TS. The results were similar to previously reported data
(Nordell et al., 2021; Usman et al., 2019). Further, it was found that DADSS contained 2.3% cellulose, 2.9% hemicellulose,
0.9% lignin, 1.69% of crude fat and 3.01% of protein.
3.2. Effect of advanced wet oxidation pretreatment on DADSS
The optimization of AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS for high methane yield was based on the statistical experiment
design of 19 pretreatment runs (Table 2), conducted in the pretreatment reactor with an initial concentration of 13.5% of
total solids. The operating parameters: temperature between 165 and 200 ◦C, residence time between 15and 45 min and
oxygen dosage between 1 and 10% of the VS of the samples tested, were used as the factors tested in the design of the
experiments. To access the oxidation effect, three runs (17, 18 and 19) were performed without oxygen at a temperature
of 165 ◦C, 182.5 ◦C and 200 ◦C at 30 min, and two runs (9 and 13) at central points of the operating parameters were
conducted at temperature of 182.5 ◦C, 30 min retention time and O2 of 5.5% to access the process variability. Again,
upon analysis it was seen that the pre-treatment had significant effect on the methane yield across various experimental
groups as the P-value was found to be lower than 0.5. This suggests that, our findings reject null hypothesis and supports
alternative hypothesis since there is significant difference between the means of the experimental groups (Table 3).

The composition of DADSS after AWOEx pretreatment at different process conditions were determined to evaluate
the effects of process parameters on the composition of DADSS. It was found that the protein concentration (4.90%),
carbohydrates (2.85%) and lipid (1.01%) contents were higher at 165 ◦C compared to protein (4.57%), carbohydrates (2.70%)

3.3. Effect of advance wet oxidation & steam explosion pretreatment on methane production potential from DADSS
Fig. 1 shows the biogas production potential from AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS material at 19 different operational
conditions while Fig. 2 shows the trend in methane yields from the 2 optimally performing semi-continuous bioreactors
at 182.5 ◦C,15 min residence time with 5.5% O2 and 165 ◦C, 15 min and 10% O2 for 3 retention times with respect
to AD1(control). The control reactor was feed with DADSS without AWOEx pretreatment to compare the effect of the
different conditions during AWOEx pretreatment on methane production. It was found that the average methane yield of
the control reactor was 72.33 mL/gVS. Further, it was found that thermic pretreatment of DADSS at 165 ◦C and 182.5 ◦C
without oxygen dosage with 30 min retention time, the methane yields of the bioreactors were 123.66 and 126 mL/gVS,
respectively. The maximum methane yields of 174.9 and 186.5 mL/gVS were obtained at 182.5 ◦C and 165 ◦C with oxygen
added at a level of 5.5 and 10%. Overall, it was found that AWOEx pretreatment with oxygen dosage significantly affected
AD of DADSS digestion, resulting in the improvement of average methane yield by 37.9 and 46.4% at 165 ◦C and 182.5 ◦C,
respectively compared to the control sets pretreated with identical temperatures but no oxygen added. The average
methane yields achieved under optimal condition 1 was 183.4 ± 2.4 mL/gVS at the 3rd retention time. For the bioreactor
set under optimal condition 2, the average methane yields reported for the 3rd retention time was 170.1 ± 4.1 mL/gVS.
Since the residence time was nearly constant after stabilization, it can be concluded that both temperature and O2 % dosage
during pretreatment significantly affects the methane yield of the materials. Interestingly, the highest methane yields of
186.5 mL/gVS under optimal condition 1 and 174.8 mL/gVS under optimal condition 2 was for the same residence time
but with different temperatures and oxygen dosages, indicating that lower temperature can promote the same hydrolysis
degree when the oxygen dosage is increased and also indicate that higher temperatures can reduce the need for oxygen
addition. The results for the control reactor is in accordance with the study by Nordell et al. (2021), which found that
only 46 mL/g VS of methane yield was achieved during the anaerobic digestion of digestate under thermophilic condition
without any thermochemical pretreatment. Overall, AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS with oxygen significantly increased
the methane yield corresponding to the result of the control reactor. Upon analyzing the difference of TS and VS % of all
bioreactors, it was found that the two bioreactors with the highest methane yields under condition 1 and 2 also showed
the highest TS and VS conversion of 43.92% and 43.15% under the optimum conditions prevailing at 165 ◦C (condition 1)
and 182.5 ◦C (condition 2), respectively. This was further the highest TS/VS ratio of 1.41 and 1.39, respectively compared
to the other bioreactors. Pearson correlation was performed to determine the linear correlation between methane yield

3.4. Influence of the different operational conditions of AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS on methane yield and response surface
modeling
Fig. 3 shows the methane yield after the AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS at different process conditions. It was found
that all process parameters (temperature, residence time and O2 dosage) had influence on the methane yield. Temperature
and O2 dosage had, however, significant effect on methane yield regardless of the residence time as indicated by high
LogWorth (LogWorth > 2, significant) (Table 5). For AWOEx pretreatment, the temperature is a key operating parameter.
The impact of pretreatment temperature on digester performance has been examined in various laboratory scale studies
(Li and Noike, 1992). Earlier studies showed that gas production yields increases steadily with temperature from 120 to
175 ◦C (Biswas et al., 2020; Higgins et al., 2017). Similarly, Haug et al. (1978) found that gas production increased with

temperature as the temperature was raised from 100 to 175 ◦C in semi-continuous flow digesters, but the increases were
half the magnitude of those reported by Li and Noike (1992). In a separate study by Wilson et al. (2011), the gas production
decreased slightly at 170 ◦C compared to 150 ◦C. A previous study reported that AWOEx pretreatment increased the
formation of small molecular weight organics, which is easily biodegradable during AD (Hii et al., 2014; Suárez-Iglesias
et al., 2017). Further, the radicals produced during AWOEx pretreatment are powerful in oxidizing recalcitrant compounds
such as lignin, which might increase the biodegradability of DADSS (Khan and Ahring, 2020).
Previous work has shown that oxygen break-down longer chained molecules into shorter chains, which can be easily
degradable during anaerobic digestion (Abelleira-Pereira et al., 2015; Hii et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022;
M’Arimi et al., 2020; Suárez-Iglesias et al., 2017). It should also be noted that higher O2 pressure also promoted the
breakage of double or triple bonds compounds into single bond, that may also enhance the carbon conversion efficiency
into methane during anaerobic digestion and produce more biogas.
Our results indicate that the high temperature enhances the dissolution of DADSS and that O2 addition helps oxidizing
organic compounds in DADSS into digestable molecules.
3.5. Composition analysis of DADSS before and after AWOEx pretreatment

the bioreactor at 182.5 ◦C, 15 min and 5.5% O2. The crude fat content under optimal conditions also reduced in the effluent

thermal hydrolysis increases the susceptibility of highly unsaturated fatty acids to the reaction of oxygen. For anaerobic
digestion to work effectively, polymers in the material must be hydrolyzed to allow for bioconversion to methane gas.
Hydrolyzing grease and fat into long chain fatty acids possess a large biogas potential of importance for the methane yield
(Wett et al., 2006).
The presence of lipids and proteins in wastewater sludge may generate compounds which are inhibitory to methano-
genesis such as ammonia (Liu and Sung, 2002; Tanaka et al., 1997) and long-chained hydrophobic fatty acids (Angelidaki
and Ahring, 1992; Chowdhury et al., 2007) through the thermal hydrolysis of proteins and lipids, respectively. Under
the conditions giving the optimal methane yield, the biodegradation of the organics significantly improved to 78% in the
secondary AD from ca. 50% VS reduction without pretreatment. A previous study by Khan and Ahring (2020) showed
enhanced solubilization of carbohydrates after AWOEx pretreatment, which resulted in a higher methane yield during
AD of pretreated manure fibers (Khan and Ahring, 2020). In this study, we further saw improved conversion of other
components such as proteins and lipids.
The pretreated DADSS after AWOEx at 165 ◦C with 10% O2 for 15 min contained higher concentrations of VFAs
(1990 mg/L) probably due to the hydrolysis reaction of the acetyl groups of hemicellulose producing acetic acid (Jönsson
and Martín, 2016) . Overall, acetic acid was the dominant organic acid in all bioreactors and the bioreactor with the highest
VFA concentration further contained the highest concentration of acetic acid (1050 mg/L). The concentration of VFA in
the effluents of all bioreactors were, however, low (less than 22 mg/L), indicating that all bioreactors are functioning well
and all digestible materials are being fully converted to methane.
4. Conclusions
This study reports for the first-time implementation of Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam Explosion pretreatment
(AWOEx) of dewatered anaerobic digested sewage sludge (DADSS). In this present study, the optimal AWOEx pretreatment
conditions for DADSS were identified based on the methane yield. The highest average methane yield was determined to
185 mL/g VS at pretreatment at 165 ◦C for 15 min residence time and 10% O2, which was 1.61 times higher than the control
reactor (Fig. 1) without pretreatment during AD of the DADSS material. A high methane yield (Fig. 1) was further obtained
with the same retention time with a lower oxygen concentration (5.5%), when using a higher temperature (182.5 ◦C). This
clearly show that both oxygen and temperature are important for enhancing the effect of the AWOEx pretreatment on
digestibility of sewage sludge during AD as further shown by the response surface model. We further found a strong
positive correlation of 0.968 between methane yield and TS/VS ratio. Interestingly, our study clearly demonstrates that
not only temperature — but the combination of temperature and oxygen addition plays an important role for enhancing
the methane yield during pretreatment. AWOEx pretreatment of DADSS enhanced methane production significantly with
over 50% increase compared to standard one-step AD of sewage sludge. This is the report showing that pretreatment of
dewatered digested sewage sludge using AWOEx can significantly improve methane production with over 50% increase
compared to conventional one-step AD treatment of sewage sludge. Furthermore, we found that the AD process can
generate 30% more methane with oxygen added compared to conditions with only heat. Overall, the two-step AD process
with pretreatment produced over 90% more methane than the conventional one-step AD leaving only low concentrations
of organics behind after the process.
